title: Did US Pay Keep Up With Inflation? 1990–2026 (Real Data)
summary: Data walkthrough of BLS wages vs CPI 1990-2026: real hourly pay up only about 23 percent in 36 years, a third of years negative, and a real-wage dip during the 2021-2023 spike that later recovered.

assertions.quote: Real pay in this series is a slow grind with frequent setbacks.

verdicts.note: BLS production-worker earnings deflated by CPI rose about 23 percent from 1990 to 2026, about 0.6 percent a year, with a third of years negative.

assertions.quote: Real year-over-year growth went negative in twenty twenty-one and stayed underwater into twenty twenty-three.

verdicts.note: Real average hourly earnings fell year over year from April 2021 to early 2023 and regained the early-2021 level by late 2023.

Derived real average hourly earnings growth was negative every month from April 2021 (-3.4%) through April 2023 (-0.3%), bottoming at -3.3% in June 2022, and turned positive from May 2023 (+0.2%) onward as CPI inflation fell below nominal wage growth.

assertions.quote: Averages can move for reasons that aren't a raise in your own paycheck.

verdicts.note: The 2020 jump in average hourly earnings was a composition effect from pandemic layoffs concentrated in low-wage services.

In April 2020 average hourly earnings jumped 4.6% in one month (to 8.1% year over year) while private employment fell 15.3% (about 19.6 million jobs, concentrated in low-wage sectors), the textbook composition effect the claim describes; the series show the pattern though they do not decompose it.

assertions.quote: Its purchasing power is crushed by cumulative inflation

verdicts.note: CPI-U rose about 163 percent from January 1990 to 2026, so a 1990 dollar buys about 38 cents of goods.
